sections.h: The opening: title, motto and the king's search (Ecclesiastes 1–2)
sections.b: A narrator introduces Qohelet, 'son of David, king in Jerusalem', and gives his verdict first: 'Vapor of vapors... Everything is vapor' (Ecclesiastes 1:1–2). The question of the book follows: 'What gain is there for a person in all his toil that he toils under the sun?' (Ecclesiastes 1:3). A poem of circling sun, wind and streams shows a world that moves without arriving (Ecclesiastes 1:4–11). Then Qohelet speaks as a king and reports an experiment: wisdom, pleasure, building, wealth, singers and many women, all tested and found to give no lasting gain (Ecclesiastes 1:12–2:11). Wisdom is better than folly, but both die and are forgotten (Ecclesiastes 2:12–17). The section ends with the first of seven calls to joy: eating, drinking and seeing good in one's toil, which come 'from God's hand' (Ecclesiastes 2:24–26).

sections.h: Times, death and the view from below (Ecclesiastes 3–4)
sections.b: The poem of times (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8) names fourteen pairs, from giving birth and dying to war and peace. God has made everything beautiful in its time and put 'forever' in human hearts, yet no one can find out his work from beginning to end (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Qohelet then faces injustice in the courts and the death that humans share with animals, asking who knows whether the human spirit goes up (Ecclesiastes 3:16–21). In chapter 4 he looks at the tears of the oppressed, at work driven by rivalry, at the lonely worker, at the strength of two together and at a king's fading popularity (Ecclesiastes 4:1–16).

common: Ecclesiastes was written by Solomon in his old age, after he had turned away from God and come back.
uncommon: Ecclesiastes is a 'preacher of joy' whose central message is to enjoy God's daily gifts (Whybray).

sections.b: The word frames the book (Ecclesiastes 1:2; Ecclesiastes 12:8) and returns as a verdict after each test: on pleasure (Ecclesiastes 2:1), on works (Ecclesiastes 2:11), on wisdom that dies with the fool (Ecclesiastes 2:15), on toil left to an heir (Ecclesiastes 2:19, 21, 23), on the death humans share with animals (Ecclesiastes 3:19), on work driven by rivalry (Ecclesiastes 4:4), on the lonely worker (Ecclesiastes 4:8) and on the people's fickle favor (Ecclesiastes 4:16). Often it is paired with 'chasing the wind' (Ecclesiastes 1:14; Ecclesiastes 2:11, 17, 26; Ecclesiastes 4:4, 6, 16). In some places the sense is brevity (life and memory pass), in others emptiness (no lasting gain) or the impossibility of grasping (one cannot hold the wind). Keeping one English word lets readers see each use and weigh it.

common: 'Vanity' in Ecclesiastes means pride or conceit.
uncommon: Hevel in Ecclesiastes means 'absurd': a gap between what should happen and what does (Fox).

sections.b: Ecclesiastes never names Solomon, but its speaker is 'son of David, king in Jerusalem' (Ecclesiastes 1:1) and tells of a reign that matches Solomon's: wisdom beyond all before him, houses, vineyards, parks, pools, slaves, herds, gold, singers and many women (Ecclesiastes 1:16; Ecclesiastes 2:4–9; compare 1 Kings 3:12; 1 Kings 10:14–29; 1 Kings 11:3). Tradition took the book as Solomon's late reflection, and the Targum tells that he was driven from his throne for his pride (Targum of Qohelet 1:12). Most modern scholars think a later sage used Solomon's role for the experiment of chapters 1–2: if the wisest and richest of kings found no lasting gain, no one would. After chapter 2 the royal voice disappears.

sections.b: Qohelet is a wise man testing wisdom. He uses it to explore everything (Ecclesiastes 1:13), and finds that 'where wisdom is great, frustration is great' (Ecclesiastes 1:18). He grants what Proverbs teaches: 'wisdom gives a gain over folly, like the gain that light gives over darkness' (Ecclesiastes 2:13). But the wise die like fools and are forgotten (Ecclesiastes 2:14–16), and wisdom cannot see the whole of God's work (Ecclesiastes 3:11). So wisdom is better, but it is not a way to gain control. Its proper end is the fear of God (Ecclesiastes 3:14).

sections.h: Toil, gain and share in Ecclesiastes
sections.b: Ecclesiastes asks about work more directly than any other book of the Bible. Its first question is 'What gain is there for a person in all his toil?' (Ecclesiastes 1:3). The king's great works give joy while they are done, which is his 'share', but leave no 'gain' (Ecclesiastes 2:10–11). Toil passes to an heir who may be a fool (Ecclesiastes 2:18–21), keeps the worker awake at night (Ecclesiastes 2:23), and is often driven by rivalry with the neighbor (Ecclesiastes 4:4). The man who works alone never asks whom it is for (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Yet the same toil, received as a gift, is good: 'There is nothing good for a person but to eat and drink and let himself see good in his toil' (Ecclesiastes 2:24; compare Ecclesiastes 3:13, 22). Monks read these chapters as a call to leave worldly work; Luther and the Reformers read them as a call to do one's work gladly before God.

uncommon: Ecclesiastes 4:4 makes envy the hidden engine of most human work, an idea close to the Greek poet Hesiod's 'good strife'.

sections.b: Qohelet's sharpest words about death come early. 'One fate meets every one of them', wise and fool (Ecclesiastes 2:14), and 'how the wise man dies along with the fool!' (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Humans and animals have one breath and go to 'one place': 'Everything came from the dust, and everything goes back to the dust' (Ecclesiastes 3:19–20). Then comes the question 'Who knows whether the spirit of human beings goes up above, and whether the spirit of animals goes down below to the earth?' (Ecclesiastes 3:21). Readers differ over whether Qohelet denies life after death, questions a popular belief, or affirms (with the Masoretic vowels and Ecclesiastes 12:7) that the human spirit goes to God. The question, with Ecclesiastes 9:5 and 9:10, is a center of Christian debate about the state of the dead.
sections.refs: Ecclesiastes 2:14–16; Ecclesiastes 3:18–21; Ecclesiastes 9:5; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Ecclesiastes 12:7; Genesis 3:19; Psalm 49:10–15

sections.b: Qohelet's poem of the generations, sun, wind and streams (Ecclesiastes 1:4–7) pictures a creation that is stable but restless, moving in circles without arriving. It answers Psalm 19 and Psalm 104, where the sun runs with joy and the waters praise God. Later he says that God has made everything beautiful in its time (Ecclesiastes 3:11) and that God's works stand forever (Ecclesiastes 3:14). His use of Genesis 2–3 is close: the king plants a garden with every fruit tree (Ecclesiastes 2:4–6; Genesis 2:8–10), and all return to the dust (Ecclesiastes 3:20; Genesis 3:19).

sections.b: The poem of times (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8) and the reflection after it teach that the seasons of life are set by God, not by human choice. 'Everything he has made beautiful in its time', yet no one can find out his work 'from the beginning to the end' (Ecclesiastes 3:11). What God does 'will be forever' and cannot be added to or taken from, 'so that people will fear him' (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Qohelet's 'fate' (miqreh, Ecclesiastes 2:14; Ecclesiastes 3:19) is not a blind Fate but death, the end that meets all. Readers differ over whether the poem teaches wise timing or humble acceptance.

sections.h: Wickedness in the place of judgment (Ecclesiastes 3:16–17; 4:1)
sections.b: Qohelet reports what he sees: 'wickedness was there in the place of judgment' (Ecclesiastes 3:16), and the oppressed weep 'with no one to comfort them' while their oppressors hold power (Ecclesiastes 4:1). He affirms that 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked' (Ecclesiastes 3:17), without saying when or how. He calls for no reform and offers no comfort; his witness is to see clearly. The rabbis read 'God seeks out what is pursued' (Ecclesiastes 3:15) as God taking the side of the persecuted (Leviticus Rabbah 27:5).

Qohelet tried wine as part of his test of pleasure, but 'while my mind kept steering by wisdom' (Ecclesiastes 2:3): the experiment was not drunkenness. Wine belongs to the list of joys that give no lasting gain (Ecclesiastes 2:11), yet later he counts it among God's good gifts (Ecclesiastes 9:7; Ecclesiastes 10:19).

Qohelet 'planted' vineyards and parks with every kind of fruit tree and made pools to water them (Ecclesiastes 2:4–6), in words that recall God planting the garden of Eden with every tree and a river to water it (Genesis 2:8–10). His word for park, pardes, is the Persian loanword behind 'paradise'. Some scholars read the passage as a human attempt to rebuild Eden, which ends, like Adam's story, in dust (Ecclesiastes 3:20; Genesis 3:19).

Two Persian loanwords help date Ecclesiastes: pardes, 'park' (Ecclesiastes 2:5; also Nehemiah 2:8; Song of Songs 4:13), and pitgam, 'sentence, decree' (Ecclesiastes 8:11; also Esther 1:20). The book also uses medinah for a province (Ecclesiastes 2:8; Ecclesiastes 5:8), the administrative word of the Persian empire. Most scholars therefore date the book no earlier than the Persian period.

sections.b: The phrase 'under the sun' appears in Phoenician royal tomb inscriptions from Sidon (about 500–450 BC). The royal autobiography of Ecclesiastes 1:12–2:26 resembles ancient royal inscriptions and Akkadian 'fictional autobiographies' (Longman). The three-ply cord of Ecclesiastes 4:12 appears in the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and Huwawa (Shaffer), and the call to eat and drink (Ecclesiastes 2:24) is often compared with the ale-wife Siduri's advice to Gilgamesh and with the Egyptian harpers' songs. Greek parallels include Hesiod on rivalry (Ecclesiastes 4:4) and the poets' saying that it is best never to be born (Ecclesiastes 4:2–3).

Qohelet's pictures of two together, lifting each other up, keeping warm, standing against an attacker, and the three-ply cord (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12) are not only about marriage; they fit partners at work and travelers on the road. But Jewish and Christian readers have long applied them to husband and wife, and Christian weddings often add that God is the third strand. Genesis says the same of the first couple: 'It is not good for the man to be by himself' (Genesis 2:18).

sections.h: The poor wise youth and the old king (Ecclesiastes 4:13–16)
sections.b: Qohelet's brief story of a poor, wise young man who rises from prison to replace a foolish old king, only to be forgotten by the next generation (Ecclesiastes 4:13–16), teaches that wisdom is better than rank and that royal favor does not last. Readers have seen Joseph, David or Jeroboam in it; the Talmud reads it of the good and evil impulses within a person (Bavli Nedarim 32b).

Genesis sets humans apart as made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–28). Ecclesiastes says that in death 'Humans have no edge over animals': they share one breath and return to the same dust (Ecclesiastes 3:19–20). Most readers take this as a statement about death, made to humble human pride, not a denial of human dignity; Ecclesiastes 3:11 says that God has put 'forever' in human hearts.

sections.h: Hating life and praising the dead (Ecclesiastes 2:17; 4:2–3)
sections.b: Qohelet says 'So I hated life' (Ecclesiastes 2:17) and counts the dead happier than the living and the unborn happier than both (Ecclesiastes 4:2–3), as Job and Jeremiah cursed the day of their birth (Job 3:11–16; Jeremiah 20:14–18). The Bible lets such words stand. Qohelet does not stay there: he goes on to commend the daily gifts of life and later says the living have hope (Ecclesiastes 9:4).
